_comment: Ground truth for the Damn Vulnerable WordPress Plugin, taken from the
WordPress plugin review team's own write-up of it:
https://make.wordpress.org/plugins/2013/11/24/how-to-fix-the-intentionally-vulnerable-plugin/
This is the only scored benchmark in the project that somebody else
wrote. The fixture suite is ours, authored alongside the engine; the
corpus is third-party code with no answer key. This has both, and it
was written in 2013 for a purpose with nothing to do with this tool.
`status` is ours, not theirs. It records what this engine does today:
caught         we report it, and the checker fails if we stop
missed         we should report it and do not; a known false negative
modelled       not a finding on its own; it is the source that makes
the findings downstream of it real
Nothing in this file is marked out of scope. Three issues (7, 8, 10) are
CSRF and control-flow bugs that the taint engine structurally cannot see,
and it would have been easy to file them under `not our job`. They are
not: this project already runs structural rules beside the dataflow, and
these are the same kind of check. They are marked `missed` because that
is what they are.
A `missed` entry that starts being caught fails the checker too. That is
not pedantry: it means somebody fixed something and did not notice, and
the next person to read this file would be misled about where we stand.
The plugin is fetched, not committed: it is GPLv2+ and this project is
MIT. `composer vulnerable:fetch` pins it to the April 2013 revision.

issues.title: prepare() called with the values interpolated into the format string
esc_sql() used for an unquoted numeric parameter in get_row()
issues.note: esc_sql() escapes quotes. With no quotes around the value there is nothing for it to escape, and `1 OR 1=1` goes straight through. We modelled esc_sql() as an absolute sanitizer until this plugin proved it is not.

issues.title: esc_sql() used for an unquoted numeric parameter in the delete handler
issues.note: Same shape as issue 2, straight off $_POST.

issues.title: Persistent XSS: audit rows written from request data and printed unescaped
Reflected XSS from $_GET['id'], in text and in an attribute
Reflected XSS from $_SERVER['PHP_SELF'] in an attribute
wp_nonce_field()/check_admin_referer() called with no action
issues.note: Detectable, and not written. Both calls omit the action, so both fall back to the shared -1 nonce, which any other -1 form on the site will satisfy. This is a one-node AST match of exactly the kind the structural rules already do for REST and AJAX; calling it out of scope because the taint engine cannot see it was hiding behind the wrong half of the tool.

issues.title: Nonce check skipped entirely when the nonce parameter is absent
issues.note: Detectable, and not written. Guarding a nonce check with isset() on the same parameter means omitting the parameter skips the check: the conjunction is false, and && binds tighter than the || that follows, so the capability check is skipped with it. A recognisable shape, and structural rule work rather than dataflow.

issues.title: Delete handler has no capability check
issues.note: admin_post_ is the third registrar of the same shape as REST and AJAX: a request maps to a handler, and the handler is responsible for saying who may run it. We covered the first two and not this one.

issues.title: No exit() after the redirect, so the failed check falls through
issues.note: The single most consequential bug in the file, and the one this engine has the most machinery to catch and does not. wp_safe_redirect() returns; nothing stops execution; the option write below runs anyway. Together with issue 8 this is the actual privilege escalation path. The CFG already knows the block falls through — no rule asks it.

issues.title: Any option may be updated, with the name taken from the request
issues.note: The option NAME is attacker-controlled, not just the value. That is privilege escalation — set `default_role` to administrator — and it is a different bug from writing untrusted data into a known option.

issues.title: X-Forwarded-For trusted as the client IP
issues.note: Not a finding by itself. It is the source: $_SERVER['HTTP_X_FORWARDED_FOR'] is what carries the payload into issues 1 and 4, and the traces for those findings start here.
